content: Monosodium glutamate (MSG), also known as sodium glutamate, is a sodium salt derived from glutamic acid, a naturally occurring amino acid. It is commonly marketed as a flavor enhancer and is identified by the European Union food additive code E621 and the Harmonized System (HS) code 29224220. Its IUPAC name is 2-aminopentanedioic acid, also referred to as 2-aminoglutaric acid. MSG is also widely recognized under brand names such as Ajinomoto, Vetsin, or Accent. MSG was first isolated in 1907, despite its use in traditional Asian cuisine through ingredients naturally rich in glutamate. The Japanese Ajinomoto Corporation patented MSG in 1909. In its pure form, MSG appears as a white crystalline powder. When dissolved in water or saliva, it dissociates into sodium cations and glutamate anions. Glutamate, the anionic form of glutamic acid, is a naturally occurring amino acid. Under standard temperature and pressure conditions, MSG is chemically stable but reacts with strong oxidizing agents. It exists in two chiral enantiomers, but only the naturally occurring L-glutamate form is used as a flavor enhancer due to its functional properties. The Ajinomoto company was established to manufacture and market MSG in Japan, with the name Ajinomoto translating to essence of taste. MSG was introduced to the United States in 1947 under the brand name Accent. Modern commercial production of MSG involves the fermentation of starch, sugar beets, sugar cane, or molasses. By 2001, global sales of MSG reached 5 million metric tons, with an annual growth rate of 4% projected. MSG is now widely used in processed foods, including canned soups, stock cubes, condiments like barbecue sauce, frozen dinners, flavored snack foods, fast food, and instant meal seasonings such as those for instant noodles. Only the L-glutamate enantiomer has flavor-enhancing properties. MSG contains a higher proportion of L-glutamate (approximately 6%) compared to the free glutamate ions found in naturally occurring foods. Fermented products like soy sauce, steak sauce, and Worcestershire sauce have comparable levels of glutamate to foods with added MSG. However, the glutamate in these brewed products may include 5% or more of the D-enantiomer. The use of MSG as a food ingredient has been the subject of health-related controversy. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires that MSG be explicitly identified as monosodium glutamate in the ingredient list of food labels. If MSG is part of a spice mix purchased from another company, the manufacturer must list all ingredients in the mix, including MSG. Some companies may use vague terms like flavorings or spices to describe ingredients containing MSG, which violates FDA regulations. If questioned, these companies would be required to update their labels. MSG is only one of several forms of free glutamate used in foods. Free glutamate may also be present in other additives, such as hydrolyzed vegetable proteins, autolyzed yeast, hydrolyzed yeast, yeast extract, soy extracts, protein isolates, and terms like spices or natural flavorings. Additives like disodium inosinate and disodium guanylate are effective only in synergy with MSG-containing ingredients and may indicate the presence of MSG in a product. For this reason, the FDA considers labels such as No MSG or No Added MSG misleading if the food contains ingredients that are sources of free glutamate, such as hydrolyzed protein. In 1993, the FDA proposed adding the phrase (contains glutamate) to the names of certain protein hydrolysates with substantial amounts of glutamate. For example, hydrolyzed soy protein would need to be labeled as hydrolyzed soy protein (contains glutamate). In 1994, the FDA received a citizen's petition requesting mandatory labeling of MSG and related substances in manufactured and processed foods. The petition also called for the amount of free glutamic acid or MSG to be stated on labels, along with a warning that MSG may be harmful to certain individuals, similar to warnings for aspartame in products for phenylketonurics. The FDA has not yet acted on this petition. In Europe, MSG is identified by the E number E621. In Australia and New Zealand, food standards require that the presence of MSG as a food additive be labeled. The label must include the additive's class name (e.g., flavor enhancer) followed by either its name (e.g., MSG) or its International Numbering System (INS) number (e.g., 621).
